title: Ox
description: Common bovine draft and riding animal
wiki_lead:
An ox (pl.: oxen), also known as a steer or bullock (in British, Australian, and Indian English), is a large bovine, trained and used as a draft animal. Oxen are commonly castrated adult male cattle, because castration inhibits testosterone and aggression, which makes the males docile and safer to work with. Cows (intact females) or bulls (intact males) may also be used in some areas.
Oxen are used for ploughing, for transport (pulling carts, hauling wagons, and even riding), for threshing grain by trampling, and for powering machines that grind grain or supply irrigation among other purposes. Oxen may be also used to skid logs in forests, particularly in low-impact, select-cut logging.
Oxen are usually yoked in pairs. Light work such as carting household items on good roads might require just one pair, while for heavier work, further pairs would be added as necessary. A team used for a heavy load over difficult ground might exceed nine or ten pairs.
Oxen are thought to have first been harnessed and put to work around 4000 BC.

Etymology
The word ox derives from the reconstructed Proto-Indo-European root *uks-en-, translated as 'male animal'. The term has been reconstructed using cognates from several separate branches of Indo-European languages: Welsh ych meaning 'ox', Middle Irish oss 'stag', Avestan uxshan- 'ox' or 'bull', and Sanskrit uksa, inferred to relate to cattle. Welsh and Middle Irish are Celtic languages, while Avestan and Sanskrit are Indo-Iranian languages. The wide usage of the root throughout Eurasia serves as evidence for the existence of shared Proto-Indo-European ancestry.
The prefix *uks-en- is possibly from the reconstructed root *uks- which has been translated as 'to sprinkle'. It could also relate to ugw-, relating to 'wet' or 'moist'. Therefore, *uks-en- could be translated to 'besprinkler'. Another interpretation could take the en- root, meaning 'onto', into account, translating the term as 'to sprinkle onto'.
The reconstructed Proto-Germanic word *ukhson, meaning 'ox', derives from the Proto-Indo-European root *uks-en-. The word led to terms meaning 'ox' used in East, West, and North Germanic languages: Old Norse oxi, Old Frisian oxa, Middle Dutch osse, Old High German ohso, German ochse, and Gothic auhsa. The term then evolved into the Old English oxa and later into Middle English oxe. Its current form, ox, has come to mean 'a domestic bovine mammal' or, broadly, 'a bovine mammal'. Some definitions specify an ox as a "bull that has been castrated".


Training

In the New England tradition, young castrated cattle selected for draft are known as working steers and are trained from a young age. Their teamster makes or buys as many as a dozen yokes of different sizes for each animal as it grows. The steers are normally considered fully trained at the age of four and only then become known as oxen.

grok_lead: An ox (plural: oxen) is commonly the castrated adult male of domestic cattle ( Bos taurus), a large ruminant ungulate in the family Bovidae, trained primarily as a draft animal for agricultural labor such as plowing fields, hauling loads, and logging. Unlike intact bulls, oxen exhibit a calmer temperament due to castration, which occurs typically before sexual maturity to enhance docility and growth efficiency, allowing them to reach weights of 1,000 to 3,000 pounds (450â1,360 kg) at maturity. Domesticated from the wild aurochs ( Bos primigenius) around 10,000 years ago in the Near East, oxen have been integral to human agriculture since the Neolithic period, enabling the expansion of farming through their reliable draft power. Their use spread globally, from ancient Mesopotamia and Egyptâwhere they powered early plowsâto medieval Europe and the 19th-century American West, where breeds like Shorthorn and Devon were favored for their endurance on rough terrain and ability to subsist on coarse forage like sagebrush. Oxen offered economic advantages over horses, costing about one-fifth as much in the 19th-century American West (a yoke at $20 versus $100 for horses) and providing dual utility as draft animals and eventual meat sources after their 12â15-year working life. In modern times, mechanization has largely supplanted oxen in industrialized agriculture, but they persist in sustainable farming, cultural events, and developing regions, with approximately 1,791 oxen owned by 423 teamsters across 39 U.S. states as of 2022, often for logging, exhibitions, and organic plowing to preserve soil health. Globally, oxen remain vital in parts of Asia and Africa for smallholder farms, supporting food security without fossil fuels, while their historical role underscores the transition from animal to mechanical power in human civilization.
